name: Rafael Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take the first call when someone's had a car accident, for an insurance company. They ring up shaken, and I go through the script: where it happened, who was driving, photos, the other driver's details. The call centre's in a business park by the motorway junction, about twenty minutes on the bus. I like that the script tells you exactly what to do, so you don't have to guess.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how are you finding it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A bit over a year. I'm not great at the typing while they're talking, so my notes are short and the claims team sends some back. They've got a new system that writes the notes for you while you listen, but I haven't switched it on, I don't trust what it writes. I live with my girlfriend Lena, who works at a dry cleaner's, and we've got maybe two or three weeks of money if something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So more or less what we've got now, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, it's a tool, it does some bits. At work I'd say the note-writing thing was never going to replace someone talking to a person who's just crashed. I don't really post online, so I'd just say it in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm not relaxed even in that one. My notes get sent back, my manager has mentioned it twice, and there's only one other big call centre within an hour. If I lose this job, we're behind on rent within a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try harder on the notes, maybe stay ten minutes after to tidy them up. I'd cut the takeaways and the second streaming account, that's about sixty a month. And I'd ask my manager what exactly I need to fix, because I've been avoiding that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, the same as now. It's a low-level thing in my stomach most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You haven't switched on the note-writing tool. Would that help with the notes being sent back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, everyone says it does. But I tried it once in training and it wrote that the customer was injured when they weren't. If the note-writing tool gets something wrong, it's my name on the claim, not the computer's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if you were behind on rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go to Lena's parents first, they'd lend us something. After that, I don't know. I don't like asking anyone for money, it makes me feel useless.

say: I'd say AI is just **a tool** that does some bits.
In the canteen I'd say it can't replace **talking to someone** who's crashed.
think: His **notes** keep getting sent back, and his manager has noticed.
With one other call centre nearby, losing the job puts rent **behind in a month**.
do: Stay **ten minutes late** to tidy his claim notes.
Cut takeaways and a streaming account, saving about **sixty a month**.
Ask his manager **exactly what to fix**.
feel: **Nervous**, a low-level feeling in his **stomach** most days.
S0.quote: If the note-writing tool gets something wrong, it's my name on the claim, not the computer's.
fieldNote: His worry comes from **weak performance**, not from AI.
He avoids the **note tool** after one bad experience in training.
He dislikes **asking for money**, which may stop him seeking help early.

steps.text: Stay ten minutes after each shift to tidy claim notes
Cancel takeaways and the second streaming account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Booking. Yeah, that sounds like my whole floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, they'll do what's cheapest, that's how it's always been. I wouldn't be angry at anyone in particular. At work I'd probably say it'll take longer than they think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think first-notice calls are exactly what goes. It's a script, and a computer is better at a script than me. They'd keep a few people for the bad crashes and the complaints, and those people won't be the ones with notes that get sent back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and hope they cut by length of service, not by scores. I'd ask my uncle about his tiling business, because he's said before he could use someone. And I'd tell Lena we stop putting anything on the credit card, full stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You still wouldn't switch on the note tool, even then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if they made it compulsory. I'm not going to be the one who volunteers for it. I know that sounds stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would tiling really suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I helped him for a summer when I was eighteen and my knees hated it. But it's real work you can see at the end of the day, and nobody's putting a computer on a bathroom floor yet. It's not what I'd pick, but it's something.

say: I'd say it's just **business**, and firms do what's cheapest.
At work I'd say it'll take **longer** than they think.
think: **First-notice calls** are a script, so they go first.
The few people kept won't be the ones with **weak notes**.
do: Keep his head down and hope cuts go by **length of service**.
Ask his uncle about work in his **tiling business**.
Stop all **credit card** spending with Lena.
feel: Like **waiting for a letter** he knows is coming.
S1.quote: Nobody's putting a computer on a bathroom floor yet.
fieldNote: He blames nobody, which fits his **centre** views, but expects to lose the job.
He would only use the tool if it became **compulsory**.
His uncle's **tiling** work is a fallback he doesn't really want.

steps.text: Keep taking accident calls and wait for the cuts to be announced
Ask his uncle for work in the tiling business
Stop all credit card spending in the household

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I don't even know what I'd say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much, honestly. Maybe that it's mad, that nobody saw it coming. I'm not one for big speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be finished at the insurance place within months, I think, it's all thinking and typing. Tiling would last until the robots in 2031, if my uncle even had enough work, because everyone else would be trying to get into trades too. I don't have a plan for that, and I don't have money to make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my uncle that week. If he said no, I'd take anything, warehouse, cleaning, whatever's hands-on. Lena and I would probably have to give up the flat and move back into my parents' house, in my old room with the bunk beds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. My heart's going a bit just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm sorry, and that I'll find something. I don't know if she'd believe me. She'd probably be the one telling me it'll be fine, she's better at that than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything about the AI side, even then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't see the point. If AI can do any thinking job, learning to use it doesn't save you. I'd just want something with my hands for as long as that lasts.

say: I'd **say little**, maybe that it's mad and nobody saw it coming.
He's **not one for speeches** and wouldn't post online.
think: He'd be **finished within months** because the job is thinking and typing.
He has **no plan** and no money to make one.
do: Ring his uncle about **tiling** work that same week.
Take any **hands-on job**, warehouse or cleaning, if tiling falls through.
Move with Lena back into his **parents' house**.
feel: **Panicked**, with his **heart racing** as he talks about it.
S2.quote: If AI can do any thinking job, learning to use it doesn't save you.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** but expects trades to be crowded.
He relies on his partner to **keep him calm**.
His resistance to tools turns into a **logical** reason not to bother.

steps.text: Ring his uncle about tiling work that week
Give up the flat and move into his parents' house
Ask his parents to cover food while he finds work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five. So the same, but with a bit of a run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should start getting ready, but I'd say it calmly. I'd tell my mates to think about a trade. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still lose the call centre job, probably around 2029, once the system does the calls on its own. Five years gives me time to get properly into tiling with my uncle before then. And tiling's hands-on, so I'd have until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start helping my uncle on Saturdays this year, to see if my knees can take it. I'd put any Saturday money straight into savings, maybe eighty a week. I'd stay at the call centre as long as they keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but at least I've got something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Saturdays be enough to learn the trade properly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, but it gets me started. My uncle says two years of Saturdays and I'd know the basics. Then I'd go full time with him when the call centre lets me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about leaving a desk job for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit embarrassed, maybe, because my mum was proud I had an office job. But money's money. My uncle earns more than me anyway.

say: I'd calmly tell people it's a **big change** and they should **get ready**.
I'd tell my mates to think about **a trade** while there's still time.
think: He'd lose the call centre job around **2029**, once the system handles calls alone.
Tiling is hands-on, so it lasts until about **2034**.
do: Help his uncle on **Saturdays** this year to test his knees.
Save the Saturday money, about **eighty a week**.
Stay at the **call centre** as long as they keep him.
S3.quote: My mum was proud I had an office job.
fieldNote: The extra time turns tiling from **panic option** into a plan.
He still waits to be **let go** rather than leaving first.
His mother's **pride** in his desk job makes the switch harder.

steps.text: Work Saturdays with his uncle learning to lay tiles
Save about eighty a week from Saturday tiling
Stay on the accident line until he's let go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. A lot can happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and people shouldn't panic. I'd also say people should get a trade, because it's always useful. That's what my dad always said anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd probably not do much for a while, which isn't smart. The insurance job probably goes before 2036 anyway, maybe around 2030, because it's a script. So the ten years aren't really ten years for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am and get the notes right. I'd wait a year or two to see who loses their jobs first. Then probably Saturdays with my uncle, and save what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, not terrible. Like a bill I know is due next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ten years aren't really ten years for you. Can you explain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AGI thing is 2036, but the stuff that does my calls comes way before that. Insurance firms don't need full AGI to read a script. So I'd be out by 2030 whatever, and I'd still be dragging my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get you moving sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone I knew lost their job to it. That's how I am. Until it's real in front of me, I just carry on.

say: I'd say it's **a long way off** and people shouldn't panic.
I'd repeat my dad's advice to **get a trade**.
think: His insurance job likely goes around **2030**, well before full AGI.
He knows he'd probably **not act** for a while.
do: Stay put and **fix his notes** at the insurance call centre.
**Wait** a year or two to see who loses jobs first.
Then work **Saturdays** with his uncle and save.
feel: Not great, not terrible, like a **bill** due next year.
S4.quote: Insurance firms don't need full AGI to read a script.
fieldNote: He spots that **his job goes early**, whatever the AGI date.
He admits he won't move until job loss is **real** in front of him.
The long timeline lets his **resistance** take over.

steps.text: Wait a year or two to watch who loses jobs first
Keep fixing his claim notes on the accident line
Start Saturdays tiling with his uncle after that

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have nothing lined up and we'd lose the flat. What would help is some kind of help to get into a trade quickly, like a paid apprenticeship you can start at twenty-seven, not just at sixteen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the scripts already do the thinking for us. I follow a script all day, and it's not a big step for a computer to do my job.

headlineQuote: I follow a script all day, and it's not a big step for a computer to do my job.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old** agent taking first calls after car accidents for an **insurance** company.
His claim notes often get **sent back**, and he refuses the **note-writing tool** after one bad experience.
He lives with his girlfriend, who works at a dry cleaner's, with **two or three weeks** of money.
He is **pragmatic**, blames no one, and sees job cuts as just business.
He tends to **wait** until change is in front of him, with his uncle's tiling business as the fallback.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because he'd have **nothing lined up** and could lose the flat.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** in a trade that he could start at twenty-seven.
